title: Jon Hopkins - Breaking and Entering
summary: Prior to his performances at the Laneway Festival, Lauren and Simon chat to Jon Hopkins about his methods of mindfulness whilst touring, consciousness and the music on his upcoming album 'Singularity'.
transcript:
UK producer Jon Hopkins joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler in the Triple R studio on 31 January 2019, ahead of his Laneway Festival appearances, to discuss touring, meditation and the making of Singularity. Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: You're enjoying a very well-made cup of tea, apparently, by our receptionist, Zoran Ilievski.

Jon: Spectacularly strong and delicious.

Simon: Last week we had James Blake with us, talking about the unique pressures and conditions musicians face these days. You've addressed these in fascinating ways too. You spent two years doing over a hundred and sixty-five shows around Immunity, the 2013 record we were just listening to. What physical and emotional state did you find yourself in?

Jon: It was a funny one. I'm not sure I'd recommend it. At the same time as being filled with euphoria and amazing experiences, it's just impossible to live healthily. It doesn't matter how good your intentions are. If you play at one or two in the morning, then you've got to try and calm down enough to sleep, then get up again for your flight, and there's alcohol everywhere. What other job do you go into and all of your favourite booze is just laid out for you? It seems great, of course, and it has its moments, but I have to say I'm not complaining about any of this, because it is still the best job I could possibly imagine having and I'm always grateful. It's just impossible to do it and remain completely healthy, so you have to take gaps. You have to learn a lot of techniques for dealing with exhaustion. You also have to make sure it doesn't go to your head and turn you into someone repellent, because it's a very unusual and maybe unnatural circumstance, playing your stuff to thousands of people and having all this applause. You start to think, maybe this is about me, but it's not. It's about the music, and the music doesn't feel like it comes from me. So I'm trying to step back away from that egotistical stuff now.

Simon: One technique you've spoken about for overcoming exhaustion is Transcendental Meditation. We've talked to others, including your friend Flying Lotus, about the benefits; he even likes to create music in a trance-like state. How were you introduced to it, and what has it given you?

Jon: I think I just loved the name many years ago. I thought, that's such a beautiful name, and the way those two words look written down. I started meditating when I was twenty-one, but it wasn't TM. It was a form of kundalini meditation, a kind of yogic meditation which includes lots of breathwork, so it's very different from TM. Then, like many people, I heard David Lynch talk eloquently about it. I did a remix for him and got the amazing opportunity to hang out with him. I thought, I need to learn this thing, because he's exuding this great calm and curiosity, which is quite rare in people. I don't know many legendary directors, admittedly, but generally people who've done very well in their artistic field tend to be less curious about other people and more interested in monologuing. I found him amazingly curious. He didn't want to talk about himself at all. He just wanted to know stuff all the time, and he was very centred and peaceful. I thought, I could probably learn this thing and it might help.

Lauren: You've said it helps you overcome creative blocks in the studio?

Jon: Yeah. This is something anyone making any kind of music, I assume, must experience, but particularly in the electronic music-making world. There's a particular awfulness to that feeling, because you're staring at this screen the whole time, and that's not what our eyes have evolved to be doing all the time. It can be very uncomfortable. You're looking at grids and lines and graphs, and your ears get exhausted. Sometimes we're so hard on ourselves because we're not achieving something at the speed we want to. Rather than stopping and taking a breath and realising that might help, we say, no, I'm not going to stop until I've achieved this one thing, and just keep hammering away. I'm not even going to allow myself to eat until I've achieved some form of breakthrough on this track that's stuck. I've completely flipped that round. I will stop and meditate, or even just do a bit of exercise, or anything really, if you're stuck. I don't think sitting there trying to force your way through is ever going to work. You come back to it and find that your brain, in all its wisdom, has figured out the problem or come up with a little spark that will maybe guide you to finishing that off.

Lauren: You've also used the breathing technique of Wim Hof, the Dutch Iceman. Could you explain how that fits into your life?

Jon: I consider this to be a kind of nuclear option for anxiety or exhaustion, or indeed just positivity, because I'm pretty highly sensitive to energies around me. Particularly in 2016, when it felt like the world took a weird turn in many ways, I wasn't very good at dealing with that. It's a fact: the world is always changing and it doesn't always go the way we hope, but you need to learn resilience. I was drowning in that a little bit and trying to write this album, and it wasn't going the way I'd hoped. I hit the floor a bit and was incapacitated, feeling really dizzy and exhausted without having anything technically wrong with me. I don't know, I never found out what it was. There was no physiological, measurable reason for it. I had lots of tests. I remember going to a doctor and he was like, you should probably get on these antidepressants. Every part of me was screaming out, I don't feel depressed, I'm just dizzy and tired and I can't work. At the same time I heard Wim Hof talking on the Joe Rogan podcast. I remember thinking, instead of going on these pills, I'm going to do what this guy says, because he sounds like he's got hold of some interesting wisdom. It's a very easy breathing technique to learn. I signed up for this online course. It's a particular method of taking in far more oxygen than normal in a conscious way, so he calls it conscious hyperventilation, then retention with the breath out and retention with the breath in. It causes you essentially to get high in a way that's completely natural and beneficial, without any side effects. Within, I think, a week and a half, I was back writing, and writing much better music. My fitness had improved, and I started getting into the second element, cold exposure. You start by turning the shower cold at the end for the last ten seconds, then build that length of time up until you're doing ten minutes in the cold. The feeling that comes with that is indescribable. All these years you think, I love a nice hot shower, but actually this is way, way nicer once you get used to it. I'm not saying it's easy at first. Most mornings you're like, oh, not this, but once you do it, your body just lights up. The week before Christmas this year, for example, I was in London, and I think three times that week I went to Hampstead Heath. It's a beautiful park with these three swimming ponds that are open all year round, and you get these hardcore cold swimmers who swim every day of the year. I've been going there and getting in the water. It's about five degrees Celsius, a lot colder than the coldest shower you can get, particularly in a hot country like this. All day long it's like your positivity is actually locked in, and you output that to other people, so it's not just a selfish practice. It really feels like if more people were to address their moods, we would all kind of—because we feed off each other as a species. It really feels like an important thing.

Simon: You've said there's no comfort without discomfort. How does that relate to your work as a musician, producer and performer? What discomfort are you experiencing or leaning into?

Jon: I should point out that I think that was a Wim Hof quote I was probably paraphrasing and getting wrong. But the idea does apply to my music, certainly. I've always had this obsession with contrast within music, the necessity of darkness for there to be light. Those gritty, dirty, distorted, broken-up sounds, I wouldn't want to make an album of just those, but I wouldn't want to make an album of just floaty, ethereal, nurturing stuff either. Those two things together, that dichotomy, is a foundation of what I'm trying to do with this music.

Simon: Has the transformation you've undergone through breathing techniques and meditation changed the place of music in your life, or how you approach making it?

Jon: In terms of importance, music is where it always was, right there in the centre. But it's given me confidence. I guess it gives you more perspective. If you can expand your consciousness in any way, you can see the thing you're stuck on, the thing you're obsessed with. You start to spot unhealthy thought spirals, and they can absolutely be intertwined with the writing process. I think it's becoming able to watch your thoughts, to observe your thoughts and how they're affecting you.

Lauren: What's an example of a bad pattern you've identified and been able to overcome in your music more recently?

Jon: I've very much had a tendency to work in excess detail too early on in a project. You spend days going down a route you shouldn't be going down, and that can be quite damaging to how you emotionally respond to that track throughout its life. Now I feel like I've got a handle on that. I'll be much more likely to sketch out a broad outline and try to remember that people are not hearing the minutiae quite the way you think they are. Really it's about the overall picture. You can go into as much detail as you like later, but you've got to get that right first. I think that's something you could apply to life: get the broad strokes right, and focus comes later.

Lauren: Can you tell us a little about 'Feel First Life'?

Jon: It's the first time I've worked with a choir. That was the sound of, I think, twelve voices in the same room at the same time, which is something I've always wanted to do. I didn't really have the resources to do it for this record. It was a highly emotional experience getting to do that. I wrote it in MIDI with a crap choir sound, then my friend Leo Abrahams orchestrated it for these voices. We came up with this Latin sentence. I can't remember the meaning of it. It wasn't about that. I didn't want it to be words you could hear, but I wanted it to be not just oohs and ahs either, so it would be mysterious. Also this idea of starting with a really simple piano line that sounds a bit knackered, very lo-fi and noisy. Then a kind of bass sound comes in under it, and it opens out into an actual choir. It sounds like you're transitioning from electronic into fully human. By the end it's just voices with no effects. That's more of a description of it than anything else, but there are ideas in there I'm interested in generally, the cross-pollination of technology and retaining humanity within that, which is important.

Simon: 'Feel First Life' follows 'Everything Connected', with its distinctive, techno-driven rhythm. The transition between them feels important.

Jon: That was tricky to do. I really like the idea of finding a link between the two distinct styles, going from that hundred and twenty-five BPM, heavy, distorted banger into a zero BPM choir number. I was using this idea of a pivot note, to find a note in common between the two, and there weren't any, because they're in a semitone clash with each other. I had to build in a section at the end of 'Everything Connected' which brought in this F natural as if it was supposed to be there. It's quite surprising chordally, and then it links you over like a little bridge of sound, and that becomes the choir.

Lauren: Is that sense of surprise part of drawing listeners through the whole album as a journey?

Jon: If you think about all the lengths of time that music could go on for, it seems amusing that three to four minutes is considered a normal amount of time. If you look at all the music that's ever been made, a lot of it was a lot longer. You can sit in a drumming circle for hours and just lose yourself in that. I think it's quite fun to ignore the traditions in those terms. At the same time, you have to make sure these tracks can be listened to separately. I always made it clear from the start that if you really want a deep experience, just sit there and listen to the whole thing.

Simon: Singularity has had a long genesis. The title and concept arose when you were, I think, twenty-three. What was the initial concept, and what stopped you making it earlier?

Jon: I got very deep into programming with this old program called SoundForge, which allowed you to process everything offline, which meant you didn't use computer power, essentially. You could print everything, and it meant you could make incredibly complicated sonic developments. I had this idea to use it to make an album where every sound grew out of every other sound, like the branches of a tree. That name ties in with starting at a simple point. Some of these concepts survived to the end of it: the album begins with one note and everything grows from that, then when it finally finishes, it returns to the exact same sound. I just couldn't do it then because I had no idea what I was doing as a twenty-three-year-old. So I wrote a series of unsuccessful albums instead, which I would recommend to anyone as a sort of schooling. The kind of music I'm trying to write, I certainly wasn't able to write back then. I think you need these setbacks, just to explore what you're capable of at the time without any preconception of how it should be. You can have these grand ideas, but are they actually realisable at the time? That's a different thing, really.

Simon: You touched on the balance between the synthetic and the organic, the choral elements and the technologically driven sounds. Is there a clue in the title? People talk about the technological singularity and the advancement of artificial intelligence. Do those topics preoccupy you?

Jon: I try not to get too deep into that. When I use that word, I'm not talking about that. A lot of people will have thought I am, and that's fair enough. I also don't want to be too prescriptive, because I like the idea of a title being vague and open to your own interpretation. That said, for me it's more a statement of the record's intent: to bring about that feeling of unity and transcendence that we can all feel when we collaborate, cooperate with each other and behave nicely. Singularity, for me, is the opposite of separation. In a highly separated, divided climate, it's quite an optimistic record. It's not full of darkness particularly. The title track is heavy, but it's more celebratory overall. That was definitely a conscious decision. Going back to the Wim method, the record took a turn for the positive when I discovered that. I was making this really dark stuff, which has a place, but I realised I didn't want to add to the output. There's a lot of that stuff around, particularly in TV series. There's so much dystopian fiction everywhere. Everything is the dystopian near future. I wanted to show, even if it's escapism, just the opposite of that.

Lauren: You're creating a utopian present for us to live in.

Jon: If we live in the present, that's all there is, isn't it?

Lauren: You're here for Laneway in Melbourne next weekend, and your Melbourne sideshow is tomorrow night at 170 Russell. Thank you for joining us.

Jon: It's been really nice to talk to you both. Thank you.
